query: For the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets that are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain why their mechanical properties differ during deformation and failure when constituent count alone is inadequate? Specify a controlled comparison, predictions relative to the quinary baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The mechanical properties of equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and its subsets differ during deformation and failure due to the segregation of principal elements (Cr, Mn, Ni) at grain boundaries (GBs) during tensile testing at intermediate temperatures.
generation.intervention: Tensile testing at intermediate temperatures (400° to 800°C)
generation.conditions: Testing in air, short testing time (a few minutes)
generation.mechanism: Segregation of principal elements (Cr, Mn, Ni) at GBs, leading to GB decohesion and embrittlement
generation.predicted_outcome: Ductility loss and decreased strain hardening rate with increasing temperature
generation.boundary: Intermediate temperatures (400° to 800°C), short testing time (a few minutes)
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of segregation and its relation to ductility loss is not fully understood

falsification_experiment.design: Tensile testing of equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy at intermediate temperatures with and without preexisting precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ductility loss and decreased strain hardening rate are not observed in the presence of preexisting precipitates, the hypothesis is falsified

However, recent studies have shown that single-phase fcc high- and medium-entropy alloys (HEAs/MEAs) that are composed of three or more of elements Al, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni exhibit a rapid decrease in ductility at intermediate temperatures (400° to 800°C) (), as summarized in Fig. 1 and fig. S1. The common feature at stress-stain curves is that these alloys exhibit strain hardening and failure shortly after the maximum tensile stress is reached. Here, we reveal the fundamental mechanism for such a ductility loss and provide guidelines for avoiding this problem.
The ductility loss in metals and alloys can be related to the segregation of impurity elements at GBs (, ) and the absorption of hydrogen or helium (), which weaken GB strength and promote crack initiation at GBs, and the precipitation of second phases (intermetallic compounds, carbides, nitrides, oxides, etc.) at GBs (, ), which causes high stress/strain concentration due to the incompatibility of elastic and plastic deformation between particles and matrix. These facts suggest that temperature-induced ductility loss in fcc-phase HEAs/MEAs could be related to segregation of some of the principal elements during the short testing time, which causes GB decohesion. We examined this hypothesis in an equiatomic Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA and revealed the fast segregation of Cr, Mn, and Ni separately into GBs, which accounts for ductility loss with increasing temperature. Correspondingly, we proposed and demonstrated that preexisting precipitates can migrate the fast segregation of Cr, Mn, and Ni into the precipitates instead of at GBs, which can effectively evade ductility loss during deformation at intermediate temperatures.
